prompt: Traditional crafts such as weaving, pottery and woodcarving are dying out in many parts of the world. Why is this happening? Do you think it is important to keep these skills alive?
essay:
Crafts such as hand-weaving, pottery and woodcarving were once part of ordinary economic life, but in many regions they are now practised by a dwindling number of elderly specialists. The causes are largely economic, and although not every traditional skill can or should survive, I believe there is a strong case for preserving most of them.

The most obvious cause is price. Industrial production has made cloth, tableware and furniture so cheap that a handmade equivalent, which may take days to produce, cannot compete except as a luxury. The market that remains is small and unpredictable, so few people can earn a reliable living from it. A second cause is the way these skills are passed on. Traditionally a craft was learned through years of apprenticeship to a master, often within the family, and young people who can earn a salary immediately in other work are understandably reluctant to spend their twenties earning very little while they learn.

Preserving these skills matters for more than sentimental reasons. A craft carries practical knowledge that is not written down anywhere, such as how a particular local clay behaves in the kiln or which wood resists to damp, and once the last practitioner dies that knowledge cannot be reconstructed from the objects alone. Crafts also give communities a distinctive identity and, in many cases, a source of income from visitors and from buyers who are willing to pay for quality.

For these reasons, I believe it is important to keep traditional crafts alive, although this cannot be achieved through nostalgia alone. The most effective approach would be to pay apprentices a proper wage during their training, since this addresses the main reason young people turn away from these skills.
title: Why traditional crafts are dying out
